confirmed_claims: Direct read of hermes_state.py/_dbfile.py confirms the consolidated mechanism: SQLite unlinks -wal/-shm on last-connection clean close, and any OTHER long-lived handle's next write trips _halt_if_db_generation_changed()/_wal_generation_was_lost() -> DeletedWalGenerationError.

L16 is confirmed by direct code reading: manual-restart-required is intentional and load-bearing (capture-not-merge semantics, explicit 'stop gateway/dashboard/cron' operator message, sticky flags, split-brain/wrong-page-checkpoint protection documented in-code). It should NOT be weakened into transparent auto-reopen.

L01's core structural observation is confirmed by direct read (hermes_state.py ~1030-1057): _wal_generation_was_lost() is a pure (st_dev, st_ino) stat comparison with zero process-identity or same-process-sibling awareness; it cannot distinguish a benign same-process rotation from a genuinely foreign one.

L13's finding that pure same-process multi-handle churn alone does NOT reproduce DeletedWalGenerationError is important and load-bearing for prioritization: it means the write-time asymmetry, while real, is not currently the proximate cause of observed incidents.
disputed_claims: L01's specific mechanism citation is imprecise: the open-time deleted-WAL guard (iter_deleted_sqlite_sidecar_holders, used by refuse_deleted_wal_generation) explicitly INCLUDES this process's own PID as a blocking holder -- it is not an exemption, it is the opposite (same-process holder blocks a second opener from minting a replacement WAL). The function that actually skips own PID (foreign_state_db_holders in hermes_state_holders.py, exposed as SessionDB._foreign_state_db_holders) is used only for FTS-rebuild-holder deferral logic in hermes_state_schema.py and is unrelated to the deleted-WAL-generation guard. So there is no true 'PID-exemption' on the open-time deleted-WAL path to mirror -- a same-process-adoption fix needs a NEW ledger, not reuse of _foreign_state_db_holders as L01's recommended_action implies.

Because L13 shows pure in-process churn does not trigger the bug today, closing the write-time asymmetry is a safe, separable hardening item (worth doing) but is NOT the remediation for the actual reported incidents, which per the consolidated theory require a genuinely separate OS process rotating the generation. Treating it as co-equal with the operational fix overstates its impact.

The pure-operational counter-case (route cron/dashboard/tui_gateway/CLI one-shots through the registry more consistently, or run fewer concurrent writers) is directionally right but not fully sufficient by itself: cron's per-job open()+close()-to-refcount-zero pattern (with its own real WAL checkpoint) is a documented, intentional design (transient handle semantics), not a bug -- it can't be routed through the shared registry without changing that lifecycle model, and CLI one-shots / tui_gateway's roster-poll are explicitly documented (hermes_state.py comment, hermes_state_readpool.py) as deliberately NOT registry members. Operational tightening reduces incident frequency; it cannot eliminate the risk while cron and CLI one-shots exist by current design.
missing_gap: L12's orphan PID 1146711 (retired-wal capture at 07:59:17, invisible to journalctl/systemd) remains unidentified and is the single most concrete unexplained data point; neither the operational fix nor the write-time-guard fix can be sized correctly until that PID's origin (leaked gateway worker? stray manual CLI? something outside tracked services entirely?) is determined, since it may itself represent an additional writer-process category not yet enumerated by any lane.
verdict: Consolidated theory holds up under direct code inspection and should NOT be abandoned for a pure-operational read: DeletedWalGenerationError's manual-restart requirement is correctly intentional (L16 confirmed), but that does not make the gap purely operational, because reducing writer-process count via registry migration cannot fully close the risk given cron's and CLI one-shots' intentionally-non-registry lifecycles. L01's write-time/open-time asymmetry is real (confirmed by direct read) but its cited mechanism (_foreign_state_db_holders 'skipping own PID') is the wrong function -- that one guards FTS-rebuild deferral, not the deleted-WAL path, where same-process holding is a deliberate BLOCK, not an exemption. Per L13, in-process churn alone does not reproduce the error today, so a same-process-adoption fix (extending hermes_state_readpool.py's existing per-path, all-caller handle tracking -- not hermes_state_holders.py's foreign-holder scan -- into a process-wide 'last witnessed generation' ledger the write-time guard can consult) is a viable, low-risk, purely-additive hardening independent of and secondary to the operational fix: it only ever widens same-process adoption of a known-safe rotation and never weakens cross-process fail-closed protection. Recommend both in parallel, with the operational registry-migration + writer-count reduction as primary remediation and the write-time ledger fix as a cheap defensive complement, plus continued priority effort to identify orphan PID 1146711 before declaring the theory complete.
